title: Burak Çetin поделился(ась) публикацией участника Kiwi Hsieh : Can AI learn to land a VTOL aircraft the way a human pilot does? ✈️ Recently, I've been developing an AI Pilot prototype using Imitation Learning / Behavior C
text: Burak Çetin поделился(ась) публикацией участника Kiwi Hsieh : Can AI learn to land a VTOL aircraft the way a human pilot does? ✈️ Recently, I've been developing an AI Pilot prototype using Imitation Learning / Behavior Cloning to learn VTOL flight-control behavior from human pilot demonstrations. The current model is a GRU-based Behavior Cloning model, trained using aircraft flight states and human pilot demonstrations. In this simulation, the AI Pilot takes over in QHOVER and successfully completes the landing. Because of the camera perspective, it may not be obvious in the video, but the AI actually takes over from around 15 m altitude and 30 m away from the landing point, then controls the aircraft through the full approach and landing. The complete pipeline is now connected: Human Flight Data → Model Training → Real-time AI Inference → ArduPilot Integration → Aircraft Response This is still an early-stage proof of concept, but the long-term goal is to explore more challenging VTOL operations such as ship landing, moving-platform landing, and non-GPS environments. UAV Flight Control × ArduPilot × Simulation × Machine Learning #UAV #ArduPilot #AI #MachineLearning #ImitationLearning #BehaviorCloning #GRU #VTOL #FlightControl #Robotics #Drone

title: Sachin Jain, Ph.D. разместил(а) контент: A founder pitch I hear constantly: "our model runs at X frames per second and Y% accuracy." Almost nobody opens with how much bandwidth they actually have to work with — and that
text: Sachin Jain, Ph.D. разместил(а) контент: A founder pitch I hear constantly: "our model runs at X frames per second and Y% accuracy." Almost nobody opens with how much bandwidth they actually have to work with — and that number decides more about the architecture than the model does. The chain most people skip: the comms link available to your vehicle — kbps over a contested beyond-line-of-sight SATCOM path versus Mbps over a clean line-of-sight mesh — sets how much you can offload to a human or ground station versus how much has to run onboard. That sets your onboard compute budget. That sets your SWaP class, which determines which sensor packages and vehicle sizes are even physically possible. And SWaP class is what actually determines which program you're a realistic fit for, long before anyone reads your capability statement. A perception stack designed assuming a fat, reliable downlink doesn't just perform worse when the link degrades — it's often not architecturally capable of running any other way, because the onboard/offboard split was never really a design decision, just a default. Here's the trap: the vehicles that lean hardest on that assumption look the most capable in a clean demo. Big model, high frame rate, rich sensor fusion — because none of it had to survive on a starved link. Then the link degrades, contested or just congested, and the gap between "worked in the demo" and "works in the tasking" shows up all at once, in front of the customer. If you haven't written your bandwidth budget down as an explicit number — not "assume good comms," an actual kbps figure for the worst case you're willing to be tested against — you've made an architecture decision by accident. Better to make it on purpose. #DoW #Defense #Autonomy

title: Sachin Jain, Ph.D. разместил(а) контент: A team I worked with chased a perception fusion bug for two weeks. The lidar returned a clean point cloud. The camera returned a clean detection. Individually, both sensors perfor
text: Sachin Jain, Ph.D. разместил(а) контент: A team I worked with chased a perception fusion bug for two weeks. The lidar returned a clean point cloud. The camera returned a clean detection. Individually, both sensors performed exactly to spec. Fused together, the vehicle's obstacle map kept ghosting — objects appearing, shifting eleven centimeters, then reappearing a few feet away. The bug wasn't in either sensor. It was in the extrinsic calibration — the rigid transform describing where each sensor sits relative to the vehicle's reference frame. That transform had been measured once, on a bench, before the vehicle ever left the shop. After a week of field testing — vibration, a few hard stops, one rougher-than-planned landing — one mount had rotated by a fraction of a degree. Invisible to the eye. Invisible on a close-range bench check. But rotational error doesn't behave like translational error. A pure positional shift between two sensors stays roughly constant no matter how far away the target is. A rotational shift scales directly with range — a fifth of a degree of tilt is nothing at arm's length and eleven centimeters of disagreement at thirty meters. That's exactly the kind of drift a bench calibration at close range will never catch, and a mid-range operational test will always find. Individually-passing sensors don't buy you a passing fusion stack. The fix wasn't algorithmic — it was adding an online extrinsic self-check that flags when the sensors' overlapping field of view stops agreeing, before it becomes an obstacle-avoidance decision. Small businesses building perception stacks should treat that self-check as a requirement, not a nice-to-have. It's usually the difference between a DT&E finding you catch yourself and one the government catches for you. #DoW #Defense #Autonomy

text: Аида Гайнутдинова поделился(ась) публикацией участника Doni Attokurovich : 7 лет в IT. А потом ты открываешь LinkedIn и снова видишь: «К сожалению, мы решили продолжить с другими кандидатами». Когда я начинал программировать, казалось, что главное — набраться опыта. Станешь Middle — будет легче. Станешь Senior — вообще красота. Будет 5+ лет опыта — компании сами начнут писать. Ну да. Конечно.) Сегодня у тебя может быть 7 лет коммерческого опыта, реальные проекты, React, Next.js, Node.js, NestJS… А завтра ты сидишь без работы и думаешь: «Может, Go выучить?» Через два дня: «А C# сейчас востребован?» Ещё через день: «Так… а что там с 1С?» )) Рынок IT действительно изменился. Раньше: «Нужен React-разработчик». Сейчас иногда ощущение, что нужен React, Next.js, TypeScript, Node.js, PostgreSQL, Docker, AWS, CI/CD, немного Go и Python… И желательно уметь чинить принтер. А потом: «Мы решили двигаться с кандидатом, чей опыт точнее соответствует требованиям». И ты такой: «Понял. Пойду ещё точнее соответствовать». Но если серьёзно, после многих лет постоянной разработки остаться без работы — странное ощущение. Ты не перестал быть разработчиком. Ты всё ещё умеешь создавать продукты, разбираться в чужом коде, искать баги и переживать релизы. Просто теперь нужно снова проходить интервью, получать отказы и после каждого из них отправлять следующий отклик. Я сейчас именно в таком периоде. Ищу работу Frontend / Full-Stack JavaScript Developer. Продолжаю писать код, развивать свои проекты и изучать новые направления. А тем разработчикам, которые сейчас открывают LinkedIn чаще, чем IDE: Похоже, нас здесь много. ) Интересно услышать вас: как долго вы ищете работу и насколько сильно, по вашему мнению, изменился рынок IT? А мой главный production-проект пока называется: «Найти работу v2.0» Багов много. Документации нет. Дедлайн неизвестен. Но разработка продолжается. #OpenToWork #SoftwareDeveloper #FrontendDeveloper #FullStackDeveloper #ReactJS #NodeJS #JobSearch #IT

title: Организация Archer поделилась обновлением: Air traffic control (ATC) still runs on one of the oldest live communication mediums: bandwidth-limited AM radio, spoken in rapid, dense phraseology, where every instruction van
text: Организация Archer поделилась обновлением: Air traffic control (ATC) still runs on one of the oldest live communication mediums: bandwidth-limited AM radio, spoken in rapid, dense phraseology, where every instruction vanishes the moment it is heard. As a pilot, I witness the operational challenges that come with ATC communications firsthand. Today we're publishing a deep dive into the speech capability of ZEE, Archer's proprietary aviation foundation model. General-purpose models struggle with harsh radio acoustics and restricted jargon, and are unable to understand the nuances of aviation navigational terminology. For example the word "stick" near San Francisco is the SSTIK departure, while "stick" in North Carolina is spelled as STIKK. That nuance is not in the audio, and decoding that signal requires more than just good speech recognition. So we built ZEE differently: — A single speech engine that collapses voice activity detection, speaker diarization, and transcription into one model, emitting one speaker-attributed token stream. — Spatial grounding that injects location context so the model correctly transcribes local waypoints and procedures in any airspace. — A language model that decomposes each dense transmission into discrete, structured, verifiable commands. The result: 84% better accuracy than general-purpose speech models on aviation audio, and a 58% reduction in entity transcription errors from spatial grounding. All of it running in real time, offline, and on-device; so that pilots and controllers alike can benefit from this layer of intelligence. Every radio call becomes a permanent, scrollable, time-indexed record. And it lays the foundation for what comes next: catching readback errors and communication breakdowns in real time, before a misheard clearance becomes an incident. The next era of aviation safety should begin where it matters most: in cockpits and air traffic control towers. Preventing tragic, avoidable accidents starts by making communication clear and effortless in the sky. This is one of the missions behind ZEE, and behind everything my extraordinary team builds: a world where every single flight reaches its destination safely. Full post: https://lnkd.in/dvauVg2E.

title: Организация Department of Aerospace Science and Technology - Politecnico di Milano разместила контент: How closely do particles follow rotor-induced flow before reaching a blade? New research by Francesco Caccia and Albe
text: Организация Department of Aerospace Science and Technology - Politecnico di Milano разместила контент: How closely do particles follow rotor-induced flow before reaching a blade? New research by Francesco Caccia and Alberto Guardone investigates the dynamics of inertial particles in rotor-induced flows, considering both a wind turbine and a small-scale propeller. The study shows that the key lies in how the particle response time compares with the characteristic time scale of the induced flow. The authors introduce an induction Stokes number to identify the transition between particles that follow the induced velocity field and those that are essentially unaffected by it. A reduced-order analytical model is then developed to capture this delayed particle response, providing corrected conditions for 2-D sectional simulations and reproducing the transition observed in full 3-D simulations. The results have implications for modelling multiphase rotor flows, including applications involving icing and particle-induced erosion. Read On particle dynamics in steady axial rotor flows, published in the Journal of Fluid Mechanics: https://lnkd.in/eys6i2qJ #AerospaceEngineering #Polimi.
